title: The handoff that makes a redesign usable after the studio leaves
metaTitle: Website design handoff you can use
excerpt: A website design handoff is the repository, a content map, and a place the brand files live. Without those, the redesign stays dependent on the studio.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table. The table is where the files have to be named before everyone leaves.
caption: Name the files before the meeting ends. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a client receive at the end of a website project?
faqs.answer: Receive the repository, the domain and hosting access, a map of which file or field holds each section, and the brand files in a place the team can open later. A folder of screenshots and a farewell email is not a handoff. The test is whether someone on your side can change a headline the following week.

faqs.question: Where should logos and guidelines live after launch?
faqs.answer: They should live somewhere the next person can find without searching a chat history. Hanabi uses a client portal for brand files, documents, and project updates. A shared drive can work if it has the same discipline: current files only, named for what they are, with the retired versions clearly marked.

faqs.question: Can the studio keep the repository if we can request changes?
faqs.answer: A studio that keeps the only copy of the code, the domain, or the content logins has left you with a dependency. You can still hire them for later work. Ownership of the repository and the accounts should sit with you when the project ends, so a later change is a choice.

markdown:
A website design handoff is the moment the redesign becomes something your team can run. It includes the repository, a map of the content, and a place where the brand files live after the last meeting. A presentation of the new homepage is not the handoff. The handoff is what remains when the studio is no longer in the room.

Teams often discover the gap a month later, when a sentence needs to change and nobody knows which file holds it. The design still looks right. The company has simply rented its own site. A proper close avoids that, and it should be planned while the pages are being built, not invented on the final afternoon.

## The repository is the site

You should be able to open the code, run it, and see the pages you just launched. The repository belongs to your organization. The readme should name the command that starts the site and the command that builds it. Environment values live in a file that is not committed, with a sample file that lists the keys and not the secrets.

The page files should be readable in the sense that matters for a marketing site. The homepage should look like an outline: the hero, the proof, the offer, the way to respond. Images should be referenced from a known place, with alt text beside them. A later editor who needs to change a headline should find it by reading names, not by searching for a hex color.

Hanabi's standard on this point is clean code as a behavior, not a slogan. The build uses the stack the site actually needs. For a company site that is often Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind. The point of naming the stack in the handoff is so your next developer does not have to guess what they are opening. Versions, the host, and where the project is deployed belong in the same note.

Access is part of the repository story. Your account should be the owner on the host and on the code host. The studio's access can remain as a collaborator if you expect follow-up work. It should not be the only owner. If a single personal login holds production, the handoff has not happened, even if the design is live.

## A content map, not a tour

Walk through the site once and write down where each kind of change lives. A simple map is a list: this sentence is in the homepage file, these questions are fields in the CMS, this logo is a file in the brand folder, this form delivers to this inbox. The map can be a page in the repository or a short document stored with the project. It should be current on the day you launch.

Distinguish what a non-developer can edit from what requires a code change. That split is a design decision. A carefully composed homepage often stays in code because the layout is the design. Posts, job listings, or a set of questions can live in structured fields. The handoff fails when everything was promised as "easy to edit" and the only editor is a page builder with a hundred unnamed boxes.

Record the inboxes. The contact form, the error alerts, and the account-recovery mail should go to addresses the company controls. A form that still delivers to a studio inbox is an unfinished launch. Change it before the domain is celebrated.

[Google's guidance on people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a useful standard for the map's purpose. The guidance asks whether a page still helps the audience it was written for, and whether it is clear who stands behind it. After a studio leaves, the audience does not leave with them. The map is how your team keeps the page accurate: the offer, the proof, and the way to respond stay in words you can update when the company changes.

Include the titles and the headings in that map. Each public URL should have one obvious title. If a marketer will change a page's promise, they need to know that the browser title and the visible heading have to move together. Leaving them in two unnamed places is how a relaunch quietly goes stale.

## Where the brand files live

Logos, type files, color values, and the short rules for using them should not live as attachments in a chat. They need a home with a current version and a person who can add the next one. A zip file named final-FINAL is how a team starts using three different marks in the same month.

Hanabi's client portal is the concrete version of that home. After delivery it holds brand files, documents, and project updates. The portal is not a second website for the public. It is the private shelf for the things the team will need when the project channel has gone quiet. A new teammate should be able to find the logo, the guidelines, and the latest note about the site without asking whoever still has the archive in their downloads folder.

If you are not using a portal, the requirement stays the same. One folder. Current files named for what they are. Retired files moved aside so they are hard to grab by mistake. The hex values and the type settings written down where an engineer will open them, because a mood film will not be opened during a sprint.

The same shelf should point back at the repository. A designer who exports a new logo needs to know which file on the site must change, and which cache will keep the old mark until the asset name changes. Versioned file names are part of the handoff. Replacing bytes at an old address and hoping every browser forgets them is how the old logo lingers.

## What to do in the final meeting

Use the last meeting to perform the handoff, not to narrate it.

1. Sign in, from your own account, to the repository, the host, the domain, and the CMS.
2. Change a harmless word on a staging page and see it render, so the path is real.
3. Open the brand folder and download the mark you would send to a printer.
4. Submit the contact form and confirm the message arrives in your inbox.
5. Read the content map together and correct any line that points at the wrong file.

Leave with the map written down. A meeting that "covered it" and produced no page will be forgotten. The page can be short. Completeness beats polish. If a login is still pending from a vendor, write the vendor's name and who is chasing it. An unknown login is a known gap, and known gaps can be closed. Mystery gaps show up as an outage.

Agree who may change the site after launch, and how a change is requested if you still want the studio involved. A handoff does not forbid a later engagement. It makes that engagement optional. The company can edit, or it can hire, because it holds the keys either way.

## If the shelf is the part you still need to see

The repository answers "how does this page get built." The shelf answers "where is the logo, the note, and the latest file." Those are different questions, and a redesign that answers only the first one still strands the brand. The next piece is about that shelf: [what a client portal is for after the brand is delivered](/blog/what-a-client-portal-is-for).

When you want the build and the handoff planned as one engagement, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio designs and builds the site, then leaves the code, the map, and the files where your team can use them.
